intro: A question that trips up plenty of doctors: a very accurate test comes back positive, so how likely is it that you're actually sick? Make your guess first. Then move the numbers and watch 1,000 people sort themselves out in front of you.
note: These examples teach probabilistic thinking. They are not medical advice. A real test result should be interpreted by a doctor.
source: Gigerenzer, G., Gaissmaier, W., Kurz-Milcke, E., Schwartz, L. M., & Woloshin, S. (2007). Helping doctors and patients make sense of health statistics. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 8(2), 53–96.

cases.title: Testing for a Rare Disease
cases.story: A disease affects 1 in every 100 people. The test catches 90% of people who have it, and it gives a false positive for 9% of healthy people. You took the test, and it came back positive.
cases.q: How likely is it that you actually have it?
cases.lesson: Only about 9%! Healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones, so even a small error rate among them produces more false alarms than real cases. That's why doctors usually order a second test.

cases.title: The Smoke Alarm
cases.story: In an apartment building, a real fire happens about once every 200 days. The alarm goes off for 99% of fires, and it goes off by mistake on 5% of ordinary days. The alarm went off today.
cases.q: How likely is it that there's really a fire?
cases.lesson: About 9%. And you should still get out! A low probability doesn't mean you ignore it, because the cost of being wrong here is enormous. Understanding the odds is one thing. Making the decision is another.

cases.title: The Spam Filter
cases.story: Half of the messages you get are scams. The filter catches 95% of them, and it wrongly flags only 2% of legitimate messages. A message just got flagged as a scam.
cases.q: How likely is it that it's really a scam?
cases.lesson: About 98%! Here the base rate is high (half), so the flag becomes very reliable. The same accuracy gives a completely different answer depending on whether the thing is rare or common.

cases.title: The Suspect
cases.story: In a town of 10,000 people, there's one thief. An eyewitness saw the thief. The witness identifies people correctly 99% of the time and gets it wrong 1% of the time. The witness goes through photos of every resident one by one, saying "That's him" or not for each one. And the witness picked someone.
cases.q: How likely is it that the person picked is the thief?
cases.lesson: Only about 1%! Out of nearly 10,000 innocent people, 1% means about 100 could be picked by mistake. That's why a single "accurate" piece of evidence isn't enough on its own in a criminal case.
